title: At the Feast of Tabernacles: Living Water
summary: Jesus' brothers urge him to show himself at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem, but he goes up quietly and then teaches openly in the temple courts halfway through the feast. The crowds are divided over whether he is a good man, a deceiver, the Prophet, or the Christ, and the chief priests and Pharisees send officers to arrest him. On the last great day of the feast he invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, and the officers return empty-handed, saying no one ever spoke like this man.
story: The hostility that began in chapter 5 now shapes Jesus' movements. He stays in Galilee because the Judean authorities want him dead (7:1), and chapters 7 and 8 together record a long, tense visit to Jerusalem at the autumn festival. Throughout the chapter the question is who Jesus is and where he comes from, and every group gives a different answer: his brothers, the crowds, the people of Jerusalem, the Pharisees, the temple officers, and Nicodemus. The phrase “My time has not yet come” (7:6) keeps the reader aware that Jesus is moving toward an appointed hour, the hour of his death and glory, which no arrest can bring forward.
historical:
Religious authority in Jerusalem rested with the high priest (Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36) and the leading priestly families, called here the chief priests. Many of them belonged to the Sadducees, an aristocratic party centered on the temple. The Pharisees were a lay movement of teachers devoted to careful keeping of the law, including the traditions of interpretation that later fed into rabbinic Judaism; they had wide respect among ordinary people. Together they sat on the Sanhedrin, the council that governed Jewish affairs under Roman oversight. The officers sent to arrest Jesus (7:32) were the temple police, drawn from the Levites, who kept order in the temple precincts.

When John writes that people spoke of Jesus only in secret “for fear of the Jews” (7:13), the speakers are themselves Jews in Jerusalem, so the phrase can only mean the authorities. Reading these texts as a judgment on the Jewish people has a long and shameful history in the church, and John's own usage resists it. Some of the crowd believe (7:31), the officers are moved (7:46), and a Pharisee, Nicodemus, insists on a fair hearing (7:51).
cultural:
The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths (Hebrew Sukkot), was the great autumn pilgrimage festival, held for seven days with a closing assembly on the eighth (Leviticus 23:33-43). Families lived in temporary shelters of branches to remember Israel's wilderness years, and the feast gave thanks for the harvest at the end of the dry season, just before the rains. The Mishnah describes two ceremonies from the temple of this period. Each morning priests carried water in a golden pitcher from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, a prayer for rain and a sign of hope; and at night great lamps were lit in the temple's Court of the Women. Scriptures such as Zechariah 14, where living waters flow out from Jerusalem and the nations come up to keep the feast, were associated with it. Against that background, Jesus' cry about living water (7:37-38) is sharply timed.

The crowd's doubts reflect real expectations. Many held that the Messiah would be a descendant of David from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), and a Galilean seemed an unlikely candidate. Some believed the Messiah's origins would be hidden until he appeared, a view the second-century Christian writer Justin Martyr also reports among Jewish teachers. Jesus' learning “without having studied” (7:15) means he had no recognized teacher; a rabbi's authority normally came from the teacher under whom he trained.
literary: The chapter is built from overheard voices. John records whispering, questions, arguments, and verdicts from one group after another, so that the reader hears the city arguing about Jesus. Time markers structure it: before the feast (7:1-13), the middle of the feast (7:14-36), and the last day (7:37-52). The theme of origin runs throughout, full of irony. The crowd says “we know where this man is from” (7:27), and the Pharisees retort that no prophet comes from Galilee, while John's readers know both that Jesus comes from the Father and that he was born in David's line. The verse numbering places 7:53 here, but that verse opens the account of the woman caught in adultery, which the earliest manuscripts lack; see the note on chapter 8.

outline.t: Jesus' brothers urge him to go to the feast
Teaching in the temple: his teaching is from God
Where is he from, and where is he going?
The last day: rivers of living water
The officers return; Nicodemus asks for a hearing

doctrines.note: John explains Jesus' saying about living water: “He was speaking about the Spirit” (7:39). The Spirit would be given only after Jesus was glorified, that is, after his death, resurrection, and return to the Father. This prepares for the promises of the Spirit in chapters 14 to 16 and the gift in 20:22.

Jesus says his teaching is not his own but comes from the one who sent him, and that whoever wants to do God's will can recognize it (7:16-17). Knowing the truth about Jesus is tied to willingness to obey God, not only to intellectual inquiry.

The crowd's arguments show how many different expectations gathered around the Christ (the Anointed One, Hebrew Messiah): a son of David from Bethlehem, a figure of hidden origin, a worker of signs, the Prophet like Moses. John presents Jesus as fulfilling and surpassing all of them.

words.note: Skēnopēgia, the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths, literally the pitching of tents. The word recalls Israel living in tents in the wilderness. John has already said that the Word dwelt among us, using a related verb that means to pitch a tent (1:14), so setting these chapters at this feast is fitting.

Kairos, time, especially the right or appointed time. Jesus tells his brothers that their time is always at hand but his has not yet come (7:6). For them any moment is as good as another; his life follows the Father's timing. John elsewhere uses hōra, hour, for the same appointed moment of the cross (7:30).

Koilia, belly or inmost being, rendered “from within him” (7:38). In Hebrew thought the inner parts were the seat of the self. The Greek can be punctuated two ways. Most translations make the believer the source of the streams, as the BSB does; an old alternative reading, found in some early church writers, makes Christ the source, with the thirsty coming to him to drink. Either way the water is the Spirit (7:39), and no single Old Testament verse matches the quotation exactly, so Jesus is probably summarizing passages such as Isaiah 58:11, Ezekiel 47:1-12, and Zechariah 14:8.

Diaspora, dispersion. It names the Jews living outside the land of Israel, scattered across the Greek-speaking world (7:35). The authorities mock the idea that Jesus would go and teach the Greeks, but John's readers know that the message did in fact go out to them.

christ: At the festival that looked back to God's care in the wilderness and forward to living water flowing from Jerusalem, Jesus stands up and offers himself as the source of that water. In the wilderness God gave water from the rock (Exodus 17; Psalm 78:15-16), and Paul would later say that the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Here Jesus claims to give what the feast prayed for. The chapter also shows his freedom: he cannot be hurried by his brothers or seized by the officers, because his hour belongs to the Father. And the officers' verdict, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” (7:46), stands as the chapter's witness to him.

hard.q: Did Jesus mislead his brothers when he said he was not going up to the feast and then went?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real, and some early copyists felt it: a number of manuscripts read not yet in place of not in 7:8, which most textual critics think is a later softening of the harder reading. Interpreters offer several explanations. Many point to the reason Jesus gives, “My time has not yet come,” and suggest he meant he was not going up on his brothers' terms, as a public display at their prompting, or not going up at that moment to reveal himself. Others note that in John going up can carry a double sense, since Jesus' final going up will be to the Father (20:17), and that this is the going up he says is not yet. Still others simply read the statement as referring to the pilgrimage in the manner the brothers proposed, and his later private arrival as a different act.

All of these readings agree that Jesus refused to let his brothers set his timetable. The chapter's larger point is that he acts only when the Father's time comes.

questions: Jesus' own brothers did not believe in him. What does it mean for you that unbelief can live so close to Jesus?
Jesus says that anyone who wants to do God's will will know whether his teaching is from God. How does willingness to obey affect what we are able to see?
Nicodemus asks for a fair hearing and is mocked for it. Where are you tempted to judge someone by appearances rather than justly?
